subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Spotting shapes in a rangoli pattern

tasks_in_class.description: Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.
Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli: _____, _____, _____
How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines
Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design. Outline the object and colour.

homework.description: Try to make the following objects using shape cutouts.

time_bands.activity: Display a rangoli picture or draw one on the board. Invite children to point out shapes they recognise — circles, squares, triangles, rectangles — and share where they have seen rangoli at home. Let us Do Q1, p.44 ("Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.") is introduced: children trace the rangoli on the dot grid in their books.

Let us Do Q2, p.45 ("Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli: _____, _____, _____"): children write shape names. Bring the class together to share answers and refine vocabulary. Let us Do Q3, p.45 ("How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines") follows; children count and record.

Distribute shape cut-outs. Let us Do Q4, p.45 ("Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design. Outline the object and colour."): children arrange cut-outs, trace outlines, and colour their own designs. Pairs share and name the shapes they used.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage have rich cultural experience with rangoli; use that familiarity to anchor shape vocabulary naturally. Watch for children who name all closed figures 'circle' — prompt them to check for straight sides. Additional rangoli-composition practice is available at Let us Do Q5, p.45.
materials: Rangoli picture or chalk drawing on board

periods.activity_title: Opening boxes to find hidden flat shapes

tasks_in_class.description: Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully. What shapes do you see in the flattened boxes?
Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object (example—sharpener or eraser). Answer (a)–(f) about faces, shapes, squares, and triangles.
Name any three objects that have rectangular faces.

time_bands.activity: Hold up an intact cereal or matchbox. Ask: 'What shape is the whole box? What shapes might be hiding on its faces?' Record guesses on the board.

Let us Do Q1, p.46 ("Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully. What shapes do you see in the flattened boxes?"): small groups open their boxes, flatten them, and discuss the shapes they see. Groups report back — introduce 'rectangular face' as the shared vocabulary.

Let us Do Q1, p.48 ("Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object — sharpener or eraser. Answer (a)–(f) about faces, shapes, squares, and triangles."): each child traces the faces of a small object and answers the guided questions.

Let us Do p.47 ("Name any three objects that have rectangular faces."): children look around the classroom, name objects, and discuss why a face is rectangular. Bring responses together as a shared list.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight here is that a flat (2D) face lives on a solid (3D) object — children often find this surprising. Let groups handle at least two differently-sized boxes so they notice that different faces of the same cuboid can give rectangles of different sizes. The envelope-folding activity (Let us Do Q2, p.46) may be used as a enrichment or fast-finisher task within the same work time.
materials: Small cardboard boxes (cereal, matchboxes, chalk boxes — one per pair)

periods.activity_title: Building and describing rectangles on dot grids

tasks_in_class.description: Construct the rectangles using the sides given below.
Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle.
Look at the different rectangles given below: (a) How many sides? (b) How many corners? (c) Equal sides? (d) Describe in your own words.

homework.description: Count and write the number of rectangles in the following picture.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q2, p.49 ("Construct the rectangles using the sides given below."): children join dots to complete each rectangle from one given side. Circulate and prompt: 'How do you know the opposite side must be the same length?'

Let us Do Q3, p.49 ("Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle."): children draw outward — expanding rectangles on the dot grid. Pairs compare their drawings and discuss what changed and what stayed the same.

Let us Do Q5, p.50 ("Look at the different rectangles given below: (a) How many sides? (b) How many corners? (c) Equal sides? (d) Describe in your own words."): children examine the set of rectangles in varied orientations and complete (a)–(d). Invite two or three children to read their own-words description aloud; draw out the language of 'opposite sides equal'.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often believe a rectangle must be wider than it is tall; the set of differently-oriented rectangles in Q5 directly challenges this. Encourage children to check 'equal sides' by folding or measuring with a finger-span rather than just looking. Let us Do Q4, p.50 — counting embedded rectangles — is set as take-home practice.

section_titles: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
periods.activity_title: Discovering the square with matchsticks and dot grids

tasks_in_class.description: How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners.
Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides. How many squares did you get?
Complete the squares using the sides given below.
Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do p.51 ("How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners."): children count squares in the chess/ludo board picture and fill the blanks. Discuss: 'A rectangle also has 4 sides and 4 corners — so what is special about a square?'

Let us Do Q2, p.52 ("Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides. How many squares did you get?"): pairs lay out matchsticks on their desks and count the total squares formed. Let us Do Q3, p.52 ("Complete the squares using the sides given below.") follows immediately on the dot grid.

Let us Explore Q1, p.53 ("Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why."): children examine the set of shapes individually, tick rectangles, and write a reason for non-rectangles. Small groups share explanations; guide toward 'all four sides equal' as the distinguishing property of a square.

periods.teacher_notes: The core insight is that a square is a special rectangle — all four sides equal, not just opposite sides. Children frequently treat square and rectangle as entirely different shapes; the Let us Explore Q1 task, which includes squares among the shapes to tick as rectangles, is the key moment to address this. Additional composing tasks (Let us Do Q1 p.52 draw bigger squares; Q4 p.53 join square cut-outs; Let us Explore Q2–Q3 p.53) are available for groups who finish early.

section_titles: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
periods.activity_title: Composing new shapes from square units

tasks_in_class.description: Here is a square. Draw 2 bigger squares around this square.
Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make by joining (a) 2 squares (b) 3 squares (c) 4 squares. Show them in a dot grid.
Can you fold all the corners of a square sheet so that the number of corners remains the same?
Make a square on cardboard, cut along dotted lines to get 4 triangles. Make as many different shapes as possible by joining three/four triangles.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.52 ("Here is a square. Draw 2 bigger squares around this square."): children use the dot grid to draw two concentrically larger squares, noticing that all sides must remain equal.

Let us Do Q4, p.53 ("Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make by joining (a) 2 squares (b) 3 squares (c) 4 squares. Show them in a dot grid."): groups arrange cut-out squares edge-to-edge, sketch each distinct shape on the dot grid, and count configurations. Encourage systematic checking — 'Have we already drawn this one in a different position?'

Let us Explore Q2, p.53 ("Can you fold all the corners of a square sheet so that the number of corners remains the same?") and Let us Explore Q3, p.53 ("Make a square on cardboard, cut along dotted lines to get 4 triangles. Make as many different shapes as possible."): children fold or cut and rearrange, sketching results. Pairs share the most surprising shape they found.

periods.teacher_notes: The square-composing task builds early combinatorial thinking — children need to judge whether two arrangements are truly different or just rotations/reflections of each other, which is a rich discussion to facilitate. For the folding task, model one fold so all children understand 'fold the corner in', then let them experiment. Watch that children edge-align squares exactly in the composing task, or the resulting shape may not be a recognised polygon.
materials: Square cut-outs (several identical small squares per group)
Square sheets of paper (one per child for folding)
Small cardboard squares, scissors (for triangle-cutting task)

periods.activity_title: Making and finding square corners everywhere

tasks_in_class.description: Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same? Name objects in class that have only square corners.
Mark the square corners in these shapes.
Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?
Look at the picture: (a) Count and write the number of corners. (b) Circle the square corners.

time_bands.activity: Distribute two paper strips and a split pin to each child. Children make a 'corner tester' — hinge the strips at a right angle and check corners on the desk, book, and window frame. Let us Do p.54 ("Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same? Name objects in class that have only square corners."): children use the tester and record classroom objects.

Let us Do Q1, p.55 ("Mark the square corners in these shapes."): children use their tester or the corner of a book to check each shape in the textbook and mark confirmed square corners with a small square symbol.
Let us Do Q2, p.55 ("Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?"): children join dots on the grid, trying to find squares of different sizes and tilts.

Let us Do Q3, p.56 ("Look at the picture: (a) Count and write the number of corners. (b) Circle the square corners."): children count all corners in the composite figure and identify which are square corners.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have worked on rectangles and squares understand that these shapes have square corners; the key step here is transferring that idea to a physical test they can apply to any object or drawn shape. A common error is marking corners that look 'nearly square' — encourage children to actually overlay the tester rather than judge by eye. Matchstick extension tasks (Let us Do Q4–Q5, p.56) are available for fast finishers.
materials: Paper strips (two per child, about 10 cm long)
Split pins or paper fasteners (one per child)

periods.activity_title: Matchstick squares and corner counting puzzles

tasks_in_class.description: Use two matchsticks to make two square corners and then four square corners. Draw and show it in the space given below.
Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q4, p.56 ("Use two matchsticks to make two square corners and then four square corners. Draw and show it in the space given below."): children lay matchsticks on their desks in an L-shape to form two square corners, then rearrange to form four. They sketch each arrangement in their books and label the square corners.

Let us Do Q5, p.56 ("Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?"): introduce Murugan's arrangement with a sketch on the board. Children work in pairs with matchsticks to find how many squares are possible with 12; encourage systematic exploration and recording. Groups share their arrangements and count together.

periods.teacher_notes: The matchstick puzzle encourages children to share sides between squares — a key structural insight. Children who simply lay out isolated squares will use too many matchsticks; prompt them: 'Can two squares share a wall?' The understanding of square corners built in work on rectangles and squares supports children in recognising that every junction in a matchstick grid is a square corner.
materials: Blank paper or notebooks for sketching

periods.activity_title: Exploring triangles through real objects and dot patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself, in your notebook.
Count the number of triangles in the given rangoli. (a) and (b)
How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?
Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.

time_bands.activity: Ask children to look around the room and their belongings for triangular shapes. Let us Do Q1, p.57 ("Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself, in your notebook."): children sketch and label three or four objects. Share as a class — prompt: 'How do you know it is a triangle?'

Let us Do Q2, p.57 ("Count the number of triangles in the given rangoli. (a) and (b)"): children count triangles in each rangoli pattern, including overlapping ones. Compare answers in pairs and reconcile.

Let us Do Q3, p.57 ("How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?"): children draw lines between dots, record each distinct triangle, and try to be systematic. Discuss: 'How do we know we have found them all?'
Let us Do Q4, p.57 ("Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles."): pairs manipulate matchsticks to solve the puzzle, then draw the solution in their books.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may count the same triangle twice when it appears in different orientations inside a rangoli; encourage them to mark each triangle as they count it. The dots-on-a-circle task is open-ended — different children will find different numbers, which makes it a good class discussion about what counts as 'different'. The matchstick puzzle is best done physically before drawing.

section_titles: Circus with circles — circle and centre
periods.activity_title: Tracing circles and discovering the centre by folding

tasks_in_class.description: Draw colourful circles to complete the circus scene.
Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings in your notebook.
Try to make a circle on the playground.
Name some objects that are like circles.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.58 ("Name some objects that are like circles."): children brainstorm and list circular objects; gather responses on the board. Ask: 'What makes them all circles — what is special about the shape?'

Let us Do Q2, p.58 ("Draw colourful circles to complete the circus scene.") and Let us Do Q3, p.58 ("Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings in your notebook."): children trace several circular objects of different sizes, colour them, and note how the size changes with the object. Fold one traced circle in half, open, fold a different way — the fold lines meet at one point. Introduce 'centre' from this observation.

Let us Do p.59 ("Try to make a circle on the playground."): if space allows, children use a string tied between two points (one child as anchor, one tracing) to draw a circle on the floor or yard. Otherwise, replicate with a string, pencil, and sheet of paper at the desk. Children share what they discovered about keeping the string the same length all the way round.

periods.teacher_notes: The folding activity is the conceptual centrepiece — children discover the centre as the point where all fold lines meet, and may notice that a fold through the centre produces the longest line across the circle. If the playground activity is not feasible, the string-and-pencil version at the desk still delivers the key insight about equal distance from the centre. A common error is tracing only part of a circle because the object slips — show children how to hold the object firmly.
materials: Bottle caps, bangles, or ring objects of varied sizes (a few per pair)
Paper plates (one per child for folding)
String and pencil (for the circle-making activity)

tasks_in_class.description: Look at these two shapes (square and triangle): discuss similarities and differences. Tick (a) corners: same/different (b) number of sides: same/different.
Find the largest rectangle in these shapes.
I made one triangle, then another row. How many triangles in second figure? If one more row, how many in the third figure?
Here are some rectangles that are torn. How many square pieces have been torn from each shape?
Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd? Discuss.

homework.description: Choose any pair of shapes. Share the similarities and differences in these shapes with your friends.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.60 ("Look at these two shapes (square and triangle): discuss similarities and differences. Tick (a) corners: same/different (b) number of sides: same/different."): children examine the pair and tick the responses. Collect a few answers and establish the comparison vocabulary — sides, corners, equal.

Let us Do Q3, p.61 ("Find the largest rectangle in these shapes.") and Let us Do Q4, p.61 ("I made one triangle, then another row. How many triangles in second figure? If one more row, how many in the third figure?"): children work on both tasks; Q4 asks them to spot the growth pattern (1 triangle, 4 triangles, …) and predict the next term.

Let us Do Q5, p.61 ("Here are some rectangles that are torn. How many square pieces have been torn from each shape?"): children count the squares removed and record. Discuss: 'How can you tell how many squares were there before tearing?'

Let us Do Q6, p.62 ("Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd? Discuss."): small groups discuss which shape they would choose as the odd one out and explain their reasoning. Groups share — multiple valid answers are expected and celebrated.

periods.teacher_notes: The triangle-row growth task (Q4) is the pattern-extension task for this chapter — help children see that the count follows a predictable rule by drawing the figures on the board and counting together. The odd-one-out task (Q6) has no single right answer; its value is in the quality of reasoning children give, so press for justifications rather than answers. Let us Do Q2, p.60 is set as take-home practice.

periods.activity_title: Splitting, filling, and creating with all shapes

tasks_in_class.description: To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes from the left side to fill the gaps in the shape on the right side.
Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.
Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles.
Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations in your notebook: (a) Triangle (b) Rectangle (c) Circle (d) Any other shape of your choice.
Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle given in the end of the book. Can you create these shapes using some of the pieces?

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q7, p.62 ("To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes from the left side to fill the gaps in the shape on the right side."), Q8, p.62 ("Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles."), and Q9, p.62 ("Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles."): children work through the three spatial puzzles independently, then verify with a partner. Invite a child to demonstrate Q8 on the board.

Let us Do Q10, p.62 ("Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations in your notebook: (a) Triangle (b) Rectangle (c) Circle (d) Any other shape of your choice."): children draw each shape in at least two sizes or orientations, reinforcing that shape identity is independent of size and direction.

Tangram p.63 ("Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle given in the end of the book. Can you create these shapes using some of the pieces?"): children cut or retrieve their tangram pieces and attempt to form the given outlines. Pairs challenge each other to build new outlines. The border-design activity (Doors-dots-lines p.63) is available as an extension for groups who finish.

periods.teacher_notes: The splitting tasks (Q8 and Q9) require children to visualise where lines must go before drawing — encourage a moment of quiet thinking before pencil touches paper, and accept trial-and-error as valid. The tangram is a rich culminating activity because it draws on the full vocabulary of triangles, squares, and rectangles developed across the chapter. The Doors-dots-lines border-design task (p.63) is available as a creative extension.
materials: Tangram pieces (from the book's end-page cutout or pre-cut sets)

items.prompt: Draw a simple rangoli using at least one circle, one triangle, and one rectangle. Label each shape you have used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The drawing should contain a recognisable circle (curved, closed), a triangle (3 straight sides), and a rectangle (4 sides, opposite sides equal), each correctly labelled with its shape name.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify each shape by its boundary — curved or straight sides — and name it.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use shape cut-outs to trace before labelling; stretch: ask them to add one more shape and explain how they know its name.

exercise.description: Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.

items.prompt: Take a shape cut-out of any one shape. Trace it three times in different positions on your page to make a small design. Write the name of the shape you used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three outlines of the chosen shape (e.g. three triangles) arranged as a design, with the correct shape name written (e.g. 'triangle').
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the cut-out and identify the shape by its number of sides and corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child press the cut-out firmly and trace slowly one outline at a time; stretch: use two different shapes and name both.

exercise.description: Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design. Outline the object and colour.

items.prompt: Open a small cardboard box and flatten it. Look carefully at the flat shape. Draw one face you see and write its shape name.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A drawn rectangle (or square) with the label 'rectangle' (or 'square'), matching one face of the flattened box.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Flatten the box, trace or draw one face, and name it by counting its sides and corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically trace the face onto paper before drawing; stretch: draw two different faces from the same box and compare their sizes.

exercise.description: Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully. What shapes do you see in the flattened boxes?

items.prompt: Priya traced the face of her eraser on paper. Which shape will she most likely get?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rectangle — an eraser is a cuboid and its faces are rectangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that the flat face of a cuboidal object is a rectangle (4 sides, 4 corners, opposite sides equal).

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child may be thinking of a round object or confusing 'face' with 'overall object shape'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child may be guessing without connecting cuboidal objects to rectangular faces.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child does not yet link everyday cuboidal objects to the rectangle property.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically trace an eraser before answering; stretch: ask which other classroom objects would give the same shape when traced.

exercise.description: Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object (example—sharpener or eraser). Answer (a)–(f) about faces, shapes, squares, and triangles.

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw a rectangle by joining dots. Make sure your rectangle has 4 sides and 4 corners.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any closed 4-sided figure drawn on the dot grid where opposite sides are equal and all corners are square corners. The shape must be fully closed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Join four dots to form a closed shape with opposite sides equal and all corners square.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child first use a ruler and mark four corner dots before joining; stretch: draw a second rectangle of a different size on the same grid.

exercise.description: Construct the rectangles using the sides given below.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: Use matchsticks to make one square on your desk. Draw the square you made in your notebook and write how many matchsticks you used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A drawn square (4 equal sides, 4 square corners) with the answer 4 matchsticks.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A square needs 4 equal sides, so 4 matchsticks of the same length are required.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child compare the 4 matchsticks side by side to check they are equal before arranging; stretch: use 8 matchsticks and make two squares that share one side.

exercise.description: Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides. How many squares did you get?

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw as many different shapes as you can by joining exactly 2 unit squares edge to edge. How many different shapes did you find?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: There is only 1 different shape possible with 2 unit squares joined edge to edge — a 1×2 rectangle (domino). The child should draw it and write '1'.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place two equal squares edge to edge and check whether rotating or flipping gives a truly different shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child two square cut-outs to physically join before drawing; stretch: try 3 squares and count distinct shapes.

exercise.description: Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make by joining (a) 2 squares (b) 3 squares (c) 4 squares. Show them in a dot grid.

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw two different squares of different sizes. How many square corners does each square have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two squares of different sizes, each with 4 square corners. The answer to 'how many square corners' is 4 for each square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A square has 4 sides and 4 corners; every corner of a square is a square corner.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use the corner of a book to check each corner before recording; stretch: draw one more shape that has exactly 2 square corners.

exercise.description: Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?

items.prompt: Use two pencils (or two strips of paper) to show: (a) a corner smaller than a square corner, (b) a corner that is exactly a square corner, and (c) a corner larger than a square corner. Draw each in your notebook and label it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three drawn corners: one narrow (less than a square corner), one matching the corner of a square/rectangle (square corner), and one wide (more than a square corner), each labelled correctly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each drawn corner to a known square corner (e.g. the corner of a book) to decide if it is smaller, equal, or larger.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use the book corner as a physical reference for each comparison; stretch: name one classroom object that shows each type of corner.

exercise.description: Use two matchsticks to make two square corners and then four square corners. Draw and show it in the space given below.

items.prompt: Look around your classroom or bag. Draw two objects that have a triangular face. Write the name of each object next to your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two drawings of objects with triangular faces (e.g. a set square, a sandwich cut diagonally, a traffic sign, a musical triangle), each labelled with the object's name.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify a triangular face by checking for exactly 3 straight sides and 3 corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child look at a page of triangular objects in the textbook for ideas first; stretch: describe one way the two triangular faces are the same and one way they are different.

exercise.description: Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself, in your notebook.

items.section_title: Circus with circles — circle and centre
items.prompt: Trace a bottle cap or a coin on your page to draw a circle. Then fold the circle in half, open it, and fold it in a different direction. Mark the point where the two fold lines meet. What is that point called?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A traced circle with two fold lines drawn inside it, meeting at a point labelled 'centre'.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the circle twice in different directions; the intersection of the fold lines is the centre of the circle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: fold the circle for the child and let them mark and label the meeting point; stretch: draw a third fold line through the same centre point and describe what they notice.

exercise.description: Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings in your notebook.

items.prompt: Use your tangram pieces. Pick any three pieces and arrange them to make one new shape. Draw the shape you made and name any shapes you can see inside it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A drawn composite shape formed by three tangram pieces, with at least one embedded shape (e.g. 'I can see a triangle inside') correctly named.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fit the three pieces edge to edge, sketch the outline, and identify any familiar shapes in the arrangement.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace the outline of the arranged pieces before drawing; stretch: rearrange the same three pieces to make a different shape and compare the two.

exercise.description: Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle given in the end of the book. Can you create these shapes using some of the pieces?

items.prompt: Ritu looks at a rangoli and sees shapes made only with curved lines. Which shape is she looking at?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Circle — it is the only shape made entirely with a curved line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sort shapes by their boundary type: curved line boundary means circle; straight line boundaries mean triangles, rectangles, or squares.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Child may not yet connect 'curved' to the circle, or may not distinguish triangle sides as straight.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child may be thinking of a rounded rectangle or not attending to the 'curved' clue.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child knows squares are common in rangoli but has not connected 'curved' to circle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace each shape name with a finger and feel the curve; stretch: name one shape from the rangoli made with straight lines and explain how they know.

exercise.description: Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli: _____, _____, _____

items.prompt: Hari says: 'Every face I trace from my pencil box is a rectangle.' Do you agree? Write yes or no and give one reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. A pencil box is a cuboid, and all faces of a cuboid are rectangles (some may be squares, which are a special kind of rectangle with all sides equal). Every traced face will have 4 sides and 4 corners with opposite sides equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A cuboid's faces are all rectangles; count sides and corners of each face to verify.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace one face and count its sides and corners before deciding; stretch: ask whether any face could also be called a square and why.

exercise.description: Name any three objects that have rectangular faces.

items.prompt: Meena draws a shape with 4 sides and 4 corners. The top and bottom sides are equal and the left and right sides are equal, but the top side is longer than the left side. What shape did Meena draw?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rectangle — it has 4 sides and 4 corners with opposite sides equal, but not all four sides equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A rectangle has opposite sides equal; if all four sides were equal it would be a square.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Child may know a square has 4 sides but has not connected 'all sides equal' as what distinguishes it from a rectangle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child has not yet connected the count of 4 sides to the rectangle (triangle has 3).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child may be confusing shape names or has not attended to the side information.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw the shape described before choosing; stretch: change the description so all sides are equal and ask what shape that would be.

exercise.description: Look at the different rectangles given below: (a) How many sides? (b) How many corners? (c) Equal sides? (d) Describe in your own words.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt:
Look at these two shapes:
Shape P: 4 sides, 4 corners, all four sides equal.
Shape Q: 4 sides, 4 corners, opposite sides equal but not all four equal.
What are the names of Shape P and Shape Q? Write one thing that is the same and one thing that is different about them.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape P is a square; Shape Q is a rectangle. Same: both have 4 sides and 4 corners. Different: a square has all four sides equal while a rectangle has only opposite sides equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the side lengths: all four equal means square; only opposite equal means rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw both shapes on a dot grid before naming; stretch: ask whether a square could ever be called a rectangle and justify.

exercise.description: How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: Ananya is shown four shapes and asked to tick all the rectangles. Shape 1 has 4 equal sides. Shape 2 has opposite sides equal, top longer than the left side. Shape 3 has 3 sides. Shape 4 has no sides. Which shapes should she tick?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape 1 (square) and Shape 2 (rectangle) — a square is a special rectangle with all sides equal, so both qualify.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A rectangle needs 4 sides and 4 corners with opposite sides equal; a square meets this and is therefore also a rectangle.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Child does not yet recognise a square as a special rectangle; treats them as entirely separate shapes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child may think only squares are rectangles, reversing the relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child is including the triangle, not yet attending to the 4-sided requirement.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child check each shape against 'Does it have 4 sides? Are opposite sides equal?' before deciding; stretch: explain in their own words why a square is a rectangle.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why.

items.prompt: Sonal checks the corners of a rectangle and a square using the corner of her book. What will she find?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the square and the rectangle have square corners.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the rectangle has square corners.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the square has square corners.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both the square and the rectangle have square corners — all four corners of each shape are square corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the book corner at each corner of both shapes; it will fit exactly in all eight corners.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Child may not have applied the corner test to a rectangle, or confuses square corners with squares.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child may not yet connect the square (the shape) to square corners.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has not connected these 4-sided shapes to the idea of square corners at all.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically test both shapes with a book corner before answering; stretch: name another shape in the classroom that also has square corners.

exercise.description: Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same? Name objects in class that have only square corners.

items.prompt: Murugan made 3 squares using 10 matchsticks by sharing sides. Draw his arrangement in the space below and write how many matchsticks you would need to make 4 squares in the same way.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A row of 3 squares sharing sides uses 10 matchsticks (3+1 verticals × 2 rows, or: 4 top + 3 shared verticals + 3 bottom = 10). Extending the row by one more square adds 3 matchsticks (1 vertical + 2 horizontal sides), giving 13 matchsticks for 4 squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each extra square added to the row shares one side with the previous square, so it adds 3 matchsticks, not 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child build with actual matchsticks to count; stretch: predict how many matchsticks are needed for 5 squares in a row.

exercise.description: Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?

items.prompt: There are 4 dots placed equally around a circle. How many different triangles can you draw by joining three of these dots? Draw them and write the number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 different triangles can be drawn (choose any 3 of the 4 dots: there are 4 ways to leave one dot out, giving 4 distinct triangles).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose which dot to leave out — each of the 4 dots can be the unused one, giving 4 distinct triangles.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child mark and label the four dots 1–4, then try leaving out dot 1, then dot 2, etc.; stretch: try 5 dots and predict how many triangles are possible.

exercise.description: How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?

items.prompt: A matchstick triangle is made with 3 matchsticks. Two matchsticks are moved (not removed) to turn it into exactly two triangles. How many matchsticks are in the final figure?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 — the two triangles share one side, so the total matchstick count is 3 + 3 − 1 = 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two triangles sharing one side need 5 matchsticks in all; two separate triangles would need 6.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child may think no matchsticks were added (moving only, no increase); does not account for the two-triangle structure.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child may be counting only the shared side plus one triangle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child thinks the two triangles are entirely separate and have not shared a side.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child build the solution with actual matchsticks and count; stretch: draw the final figure and label the shared side.

exercise.description: Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.

items.prompt: Look at a square and a triangle. Write one way they are the same and one way they are different.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Same: both have straight sides (or both are flat shapes). Different: a square has 4 sides and 4 corners while a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare number of sides and corners for each shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw both shapes and count the sides and corners before writing; stretch: find a third shape that is the same as one of them in a different way.

exercise.description: Look at these two shapes (square and triangle): discuss similarities and differences. Tick (a) corners: same/different (b) number of sides: same/different.

items.prompt: A row of triangles is made like this: Row 1 has 1 triangle. Row 2 has 4 triangles. How many triangles will Row 3 have? How did you figure it out?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 3 has 9 triangles. The pattern is that each row n has n² triangles (1, 4, 9). Alternatively, children may observe the pattern adds 3 more each time (1, 4, 9 — differences are 3, 5) or may count by drawing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw or extend the pattern: Row 1 = 1, Row 2 = 4, Row 3 = 9 — each row adds the next odd number of triangles.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw Row 3 by copying the pattern before writing a number; stretch: predict how many triangles Row 4 will have.

exercise.description: I made one triangle, then another row. How many triangles in second figure? If one more row, how many in the third figure?

items.prompt: Here are three shapes: a circle, a square, and a triangle. A student says the circle is the odd one out. Give one reason why the circle could be the odd one out. Then give one reason why the triangle could be the odd one out instead.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Circle is odd one out: it has no straight sides and no corners, while the square and triangle both have straight sides and corners. Triangle is odd one out: it has 3 sides and 3 corners, while the square has 4 sides and 4 corners — or the triangle is the only one with fewer than 4 sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a property that two shapes share but one does not — that shape becomes the odd one out.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child first list properties of each shape (sides, corners, curved/straight) before choosing; stretch: suggest a third valid reason using a different property.

exercise.description: Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd? Discuss.

items.prompt: A rangoli has 3 circles, 2 triangles, and 4 rectangles. How many shapes in total are made with straight lines?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 — triangles (2) and rectangles (4) are made with straight lines; circles are made with curved lines. 2 + 4 = 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count only shapes with straight-line boundaries: triangles + rectangles = 2 + 4 = 6.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child may have counted only the circles, confusing curved with straight.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child may have counted only the triangles (2) and one set from another category.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child counted all shapes including circles, not filtering by line type.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child first sort a list of shape names into 'curved' and 'straight' before adding; stretch: how many shapes in total are made with curved lines?

exercise.description: How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, a rectangle is already drawn for you. Draw one bigger rectangle around it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A rectangle drawn on the outer dots that completely surrounds the given inner rectangle, with all four sides following the dot grid. The new rectangle must be larger on all sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Select four corner dots on the grid that lie outside all four sides of the inner rectangle and join them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child mark the four outer corner dots first before connecting; stretch: draw a second, even larger rectangle around the first.

exercise.description: Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle.

items.prompt: A shape has 4 sides and 4 corners. All its corners are square corners. Which shape could it be?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rectangle — it has 4 sides, 4 corners, and all corners are square corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the given properties — 4 sides, 4 square corners — to the rectangle (and square).

what_each_option_reveals.D: Child knows triangle is a shape but has not connected the count of 4 sides and corners.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child knows circle is a shape but has not connected 'no corners' to the circle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child may be confusing a semi-circle with a rectangular shape.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw a shape with 4 sides and check each corner with a book corner; stretch: name one more shape that also has 4 square corners.

exercise.description: Mark the square corners in these shapes.

items.prompt: Look at the shape below. It is made of two rectangles joined together (like an L-shape). Count all the corners of the L-shape and write the number. Then write how many of those corners are square corners.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: An L-shape has 6 corners in total. All 6 corners of an L-shape made from rectangles are square corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count all the corners of the L-shape (6), then test each corner with a book corner — every corner of a shape built from rectangles is a square corner.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child mark each corner with a dot before counting; stretch: draw a different composite shape and count its square corners.

exercise.description: Look at the picture: (a) Count and write the number of corners. (b) Circle the square corners.

items.prompt: Count the triangles in the rangoli pattern below and write the number.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Shape | Count |
| Small triangles (pointing up) | ? |
| Small triangles (pointing down) | ? |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: This item requires the teacher to set a specific rangoli figure from the textbook (Let us Do Q2, p.57) as a printed stimulus. As a generated item: if the rangoli has 4 upward-pointing and 2 downward-pointing small triangles, the total is 6. The teacher should adapt the number to match the figure used in class.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Mark each triangle as you count it to avoid counting the same one twice.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child colour each triangle a different colour as they count; stretch: count only the larger triangles formed by combining small ones.

exercise.description: Count the number of triangles in the given rangoli. (a) and (b)

items.prompt: In your notebook, draw a triangle, a rectangle, and a circle. For each shape, draw it once small and once large. Label every shape you draw.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Six drawings total — small triangle, large triangle, small rectangle, large rectangle, small circle, large circle — each correctly labelled. The shape must be recognisable (closed, correct number of sides).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw each shape in two sizes; the shape name stays the same regardless of size.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw on dot paper to guide size; stretch: draw each shape in a different orientation as well as a different size.

exercise.description: Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations in your notebook: (a) Triangle (b) Rectangle (c) Circle (d) Any other shape of your choice.

items.prompt: A rectangle has a gap in its bottom-right corner. The gap is shaped like a small square. Which piece should be placed to complete the rectangle?

options.label: B
options.text: A long rectangle taller than the gap

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A small square — it fits exactly into a square-shaped gap in the corner of the rectangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the shape of the gap (square) to the piece that fills it exactly (small square).

what_each_option_reveals.D: Child may not be visualising the shape of the gap and is guessing.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child knows a circle is a shape but has not reasoned about fitting a curved piece into a square gap.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child may recognise 'rectangle' but not attend to the size constraint — a piece taller than the gap would not fit.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw the gap shape separately and compare it to each option; stretch: describe the shape and size of the gap in their own words before choosing.

exercise.description: To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes from the left side to fill the gaps in the shape on the right side.

items.prompt: Below is a house-shaped figure (a rectangle with a triangle on top). Draw two straight lines inside the figure to split it into exactly three triangles. Show the lines clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid solution: draw one diagonal across the rectangle (splitting it into two triangles) and one line from the apex of the roof to the top edge of the rectangle — giving three triangles total. Other valid decompositions exist; accept any arrangement that produces exactly three non-overlapping triangles covering the whole figure.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw the first line to split the larger region, then draw the second line to split one of the resulting parts into two — verify that the result is three triangles with no gaps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use a pencil to lightly sketch and erase before committing; stretch: find a second different way to draw two lines that also gives three triangles.

exercise.description: Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.

items.prompt: Below is an L-shaped figure. Draw exactly one straight line inside the L to split it into exactly three triangles. Show the line clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A single diagonal line drawn across the L-shape that divides it into three triangles. One valid approach: draw a line from the inner corner of the L to the opposite outer corner — this splits the L into three non-overlapping triangles. Accept any correct single-line decomposition into three triangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the line so that it cuts through the L at the inner corner, creating three triangular regions with no gaps or overlaps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace the L-shape and try placing a ruler in different positions before drawing; stretch: check that all three resulting shapes truly have 3 sides and 3 corners each.

exercise.description: Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles.
